video_title: The Fed Can't Save The Market From A Crash
gist: Peter Bookvar argues the AI picks-and-shovels trade is breaking down as hyperscaler capex growth halves in 2027 (likely the absolute peak), that Fed hawkishness has peaked, and that gold/silver are at a capitulation bottom, while warning that with sticky 3-4% inflation and 6% deficits the Fed cannot rescue the AI trade and long yields may rise even in a recession. The second half is NYSE floor trader Peter Tuckman's career story plus his view that extreme single-stock volatility reflects a new retail generation that has never seen a bear market.

themes.theme: AI capex peak and picks-and-shovels breakdown

insights.claim: The AI trade has suffered a breakdown driven by a series of compounding bumps: cancelled overseas data-center IPOs (e.g., AirTrunk), NextDC being unable to get community power, and data-center supplier stocks that peaked in June-July.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Supplier/picks-and-shovels names peaked on 'as good as it gets' earnings and margins; treat rallies as sellable until capex trajectory stabilizes.
insights.quote: Those stocks peaked in June July and and on the sense that it's as good as it gets both in terms of earnings growth and also profit margins

insights.claim: Hyperscaler capex from the five largest players is set to rise ~100% in 2026 vs 2025 but only ~50% in 2027, and 2027 is likely the peak in absolute capex dollars, with 2028 at best flat and possibly lower.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Stocks price off rate of change; a halving of capex growth argues for de-rating AI suppliers well before absolute spending falls.
insights.quote: so in 2026 from the five hyperscalers, capex will be up about 100% from 2025. 2027 expectations are about 50.

insights.claim: The view that 2027 marks peak absolute AI capex is non-consensus today but likely to become consensus very soon.
insights.speaker: Guy (host)
insights.so_what: Positioning ahead of a consensus shift toward peak-capex is where the edge is; watch sell-side capex estimate revisions.
insights.quote: which which is non- consensus although I think it's going to start becoming consensus very shortly

insights.claim: Nvidia's decline is not just about Jensen Huang; Nvidia is fundamentally a picks-and-shovels company highly dependent on continued data-center construction.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Nvidia's fortunes are tied to data-center build rate, so a construction slowdown is a direct risk regardless of company-specific news.
insights.quote: Nvidia at the end of the day is also a picks and shovels company that is highly dependent on building more of these data center buildings.

insights.claim: Midterm politics threaten chip sales and data-center construction in Asia (including leasing capacity to China), which could slow builds both in the US and Asia, reducing demand for equipment going into them.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Adds a geopolitical/policy leg to the AI-supplier bear case; monitor export and leasing restrictions.

insights.claim: Anthropic's very large market cap and fundraising likely sucked capital out of other parts of the market, adding pressure on the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Mega private raises at the application layer can be a liquidity drain on public AI names; watch large private funding rounds as supply events.

insights.claim: Commodity trades linked to AI — copper, industrial metals and uranium — have sold off hard because they are in everyone's 'AI bucket', even though spot uranium (~$90/lb) has been flat all year and term contract prices (~$100) are at record highs.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Uranium equities have de-coupled from strong term-price fundamentals due to AI-basket selling; Bookvar is long uranium and sees this as positioning-driven.
insights.quote: You take uranium which I am long became an AI trade

insights.claim: If the supplier/picks-and-shovels AI trade keeps being sold, Bitcoin, copper, uranium and other AI-correlated assets should be expected to stay under pressure as one correlated complex.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Treat AI-adjacent assets as a single risk factor for portfolio construction and hedging.

themes.theme: Hawkish Fed and its limited toolkit

insights.claim: The hawkish Fed is ignoring the fragility of the AI capex cycle and falling commodity prices; Bookvar believes Kevin Warsh is markets-savvy and is watching these signals even if hawks like Chris Waller (calling for a 50 bp hike) are not.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Expect Fed chair-led messaging to soften before hawkish members do; trade the chair, not the dissenters.
insights.quote: Chris Waller apparently is not by calling for a 50 basis point increase

insights.claim: We have likely reached peak Fed hawkishness: the Fed may deliver one hike in December, but members expecting continued hikes in 2027 will be 'mugged by reality' as the AI trade reverses.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Positions that benefit from a shift from peak hawkishness (short-end duration, gold, silver) look attractive.
insights.quote: I think we've reached peak hawkishness and that maybe the Fed throws us a hike in December

insights.claim: Market expectations have already started to shift: the 2-year Treasury yield fell from about 4.85% to 4.69% in roughly a week.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Front-end yields are confirming the peak-hawkishness call; watch the 2-year as the lead indicator.
insights.quote: a week ago, the the the the two-year yield was near about 485. Today, it's 469.

insights.claim: With inflation at 3-4% rather than 1-2%, the Fed has fewer levers and more negative consequences from easing, so its ability to cushion economic shocks will be much more limited than in prior cycles (87 crash, early-90s real estate, tech bubble, GFC).
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Do not assume a Fed put of past-cycle magnitude; size downside risk accordingly.
insights.quote: the Fed's ability to react to external challenges on the economy are going to be much more limited this time than than previous um cycles

insights.claim: Fed cuts are not unambiguously good: upper-income spenders hold large T-bill/money-market balances (8 trillion+ in money markets), so cutting while equities fall hits both their wealth effect and their interest income.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Rate cuts may weaken rather than support upper-income consumption; watch money-market yields and high-end consumer names.
insights.quote: the government's interest expense is another person's interest income

insights.claim: Aggressive Fed cutting could be very dollar-negative, e.g., the dollar index falling from 103 to 93, pushing dollar-priced commodities like oil back above $100 and reigniting inflation.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Dovish pivot scenarios should include hedges for a weaker dollar and commodity/inflation rebound.

insights.claim: The 2% inflation target is arbitrary (originated with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand) and was meant to leave room for a 3-4% policy rate that could be cut in a downturn, not as an economically optimal inflation rate.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Context for why the Fed resists moving the target despite years of missing it.

insights.claim: Raising the inflation target to 3% would be a disaster that could push the 10-year yield from ~5% to 6-7%; Bookvar is confident a Fed under Kevin Warsh would not move the goalposts.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Rules out a 'move the target' easing path; long-end risk premium depends on Fed credibility.
insights.quote: the 10-year yield instead of being at five is going to go to six or seven%

insights.claim: A ~6% federal budget deficit (~$2 trillion injected beyond taxes) is inherently inflationary, leaving the Fed fighting inflation with one hand tied behind its back.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Fiscal dominance limits the effectiveness of monetary tightening; inflation may stay sticky regardless of Fed action.
insights.quote: the Federal Reserve is is is sort of fighting the inflation battle with one hand tied behind their back here

insights.claim: The Fed's purchases of mortgage-backed securities were an asset-allocation choice to the housing sector that, 25 years on, contributed to a housing affordability crisis for the roughly one-third of the country that rents.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Illustrates long-run distortion costs of sector-targeted Fed policy; relevant to housing and MBS policy debates.

themes.theme: Bond market: higher long rates in a downturn

insights.claim: In a recession triggered by slowing data-center construction and a falling stock market, the deficit could swell from ~5-6% to ~12% of GDP, flooding the market with Treasury supply.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: A recession would bring a supply shock to the long end, not just lower growth; watch deficit projections and auction sizes.
insights.quote: that that 6% or five and change to 6% budget deficit relative to GDP is going to be 12%

insights.claim: This cycle the Fed's response function may differ from the last 40 years: short-term rates could fall in a downturn while long-term rates rise because of debts and deficits — a bear steepener.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Long-duration bonds may not hedge an equity downturn; favor curve steepeners over outright long-end duration.
insights.quote: So, you can get higher long-term interest rates in an economic downturn, which is counterintuitive for many because for 40 years it was the exact opposite.

insights.claim: If the Fed backs off its hawkish posture, equities might cheer, but the bond market would likely react unfavorably with higher long-end yields.
insights.speaker: Guy (host)
insights.so_what: A dovish pivot is not a clean risk-on signal; watch long-end yields' reaction to Fed communications.
insights.quote: If they were to back off at this point and sort of change their posture, people might be encouraged by that. I'm not sure the bond market would though.

insights.claim: Historically ~65-70% of US GDP is consumer-driven, but recent GDP growth has relied heavily on AI capex; if that is derailed, growth looks much different and the Fed's lens changes.
insights.speaker: Guy (host)
insights.so_what: AI capex is a macro variable, not just a sector story; its slowdown has GDP-level consequences.

insights.claim: Gold and silver are near a capitulation bottom, likely within a day or two: gold's 14-day RSI is at its lowest since October 2023 and the Daily Sentiment Index is in the single digits, a level that typically marks a bottom.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Contrarian long setup in precious metals on extreme oversold sentiment readings.
insights.quote: the 14-day relative strength index in gold is at the lowest level since October 2023

insights.claim: The precious metals correction since the December-January spike has been driven by higher real rates and a stronger dollar; gold is now being liquidated and separating from fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Once real rates and the dollar turn, the drivers of the correction reverse; watch real yields as the trigger.
insights.quote: gold's just being liquidated and it's now separating from the fundamental reality

insights.claim: When the Fed moves from peak hawkishness toward dovishness — getting less hawkish before it gets dovish — gold and silver should respond with a nice move higher, as falling short rates also pull real rates down sharply.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Precious metals are the cleanest expression of a Fed hawk-to-dove shift.

insights.claim: Commodities remain in a longer-term bull market despite the sharp recent selloff in copper, industrial metals, crude oil and products.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Treat the drawdown as a buying opportunity in a secular bull rather than a regime change.

insights.claim: Oil has fallen as more ships move through Hormuz despite no Iran deal, but IEA talk of surpluses is 'nonsense' because billions of barrels of inventory have been lost over ~200 days — a surplus perhaps on flow but not on stock.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Depleted inventories leave oil vulnerable to upside surprises despite bearish flow narratives.
insights.quote: we've lost billions of barrels over the last 200 days

insights.claim: If the AI tech trade rolls over, foreign investors who are overweight US tech (US share of global market cap near record highs) may rotate toward cheaper European stocks, creating a major headwind for the dollar that would support precious metals.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Watch foreign flows out of US tech as a dollar-bearish, Europe-bullish, gold-bullish chain.
insights.quote: those boring uh European stocks don't look so bad here

themes.theme: Bitcoin as levered Nasdaq, and the limits of Fed rescues

insights.claim: Bitcoin has traded like a levered Nasdaq 100 position over the past 10 years and peaked alongside Nasdaq names in the summer, falling from about 90,000 back to 60,000 and roughly halving from its all-time high.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Bitcoin is not providing store-of-value diversification; hedge it as tech beta.
insights.quote: Bitcoin has essentially been a levered NASDAQ 100 trade

insights.claim: Bitcoin's weakness suggests markets are not anticipating a Fed pivot; if a hawk-to-dove shift were coming, Bitcoin would likely sniff it out first — so it appears to be trading on the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Guy (host)
insights.so_what: Use Bitcoin as a sentiment gauge for both AI risk and Fed pivot expectations.

insights.claim: A key test ahead: if the Fed turns less hawkish, metals should rally, but Bitcoin may stay tethered to tech stocks rather than trading like gold.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Pair trade idea: long metals vs Bitcoin into a Fed softening while the AI trade is weak.

insights.claim: Fed rate cuts did not stop the Nasdaq from falling 82% after the tech bubble or the market from halving in 2008, so investors should not buy equities expecting Fed cuts to save the AI tech trade.
insights.speaker: Peter Bookvar (CIO, OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners)
insights.so_what: Do fundamental work on AI names; rate cuts help some assets but will not rescue a capex-cycle unwind.
insights.quote: don't make your buy and sell decisions on equities because you think that the Fed's going to cut and it's going to save me

insights.claim: Extreme single-stock volatility (8-10% moves in major companies several times a week) is not a warning sign but a function of a new generation of retail traders and emotional, fresh money that has never seen a bear market.
insights.speaker: Peter Tuckman (senior floor trader, Trademos Securities)
insights.so_what: Expect continued outsized single-name moves both ways; size positions for it.
insights.quote: The people who have been trading for the last five, six years, they've never seen a bare market.

insights.claim: Palantir rose seven days in a row into November earnings, then fell 9% on stellar results and dragged the market, seeding an 'AI is a bubble' narrative that Tuckman thinks stuck longer than it should have.
insights.speaker: Peter Tuckman (senior floor trader, Trademos Securities)
insights.so_what: Crowded momentum names can sell off on good news and set market-wide narratives.

insights.claim: Hedge funds and family offices have abandoned buy-and-hold and must actively trade to avoid losing money in a market that swings up 15% and down 20%.
insights.speaker: Peter Tuckman (senior floor trader, Trademos Securities)
insights.so_what: Faster institutional turnover amplifies intraday and multi-day volatility.

insights.claim: Post-COVID stimulus of ~$3 trillion in 3-4 months had the market back to even by August 2020, versus ~$800 billion over 18 months after Lehman and nine years to recover; the market is up over 150% since COVID with 72 record closes in 2025 and 68 so far this year.
insights.speaker: Peter Tuckman (senior floor trader, Trademos Securities)
insights.so_what: Context for retail's 'buy every dip' conditioning — a regime that a Fed-constrained downturn could test.
insights.quote: in 2025 we had what 72 record closes and this year we've had 68 record closes
